ours.name: Honeymoon Route
ours.approach: From the Upper Dungeness/Royal Basin Trailhead (elev. ~2,500 ft), hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about a mile farther into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), a meadow-and-tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba, and Hal Foss Peak. From the upper basin, leave the trail and head southwest over the moraine to the big snow slope on the west edge of the northeast face. Climb it most of the way toward the low point of the Deception-Martin ridge, then break left into the steep side gully that gives the route its name; from its top, traverse left and climb a second snow-and-rock gully to the summit ridge. ours.descent: Climbers typically downclimb or glissade the couloir if snow conditions allow, or traverse to descend via the standard route's looser terrain; either way the exit funnels back through upper Royal Basin to Royal Lake and the maintained trail.

fktText: Description Mount Deception is the second highest peak in the Olympic Mountain Range at 7788 ft, second only to Mount Olympus, and the 17th most prominent peak in Washington (4108 ft). The fastest way there is to start at the upper Dungeness Trailhead and hike through old growth forests to Royal Basin and then through upper Royal Basin. Summiting this peak will take different amounts of snow travel or scrambling depending on times of the year and the snowpack level. There is considerable hazard from rockfall and rockslides if later in the season and some glacier travel depending on which route variation you select. https://www.summitpost.org/mount-deception/151109 GPS Track Mount_Deception.gpx 3.93 MB FKTs car to car Male Unsupported Wesley Verne 6h 23m 58s 2026-07-04 Nate Allan 8h 16m 51s 2026-05-08 Nathanael Bate 9h 0m 21s 2021-07-05 Images Log in or register to post comments Footer menu Newsletter Contact Privacy Policy Terms of Use © 2026 Outside Interactive, Inc.

ours.name: North Slopes
ours.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt swit
ours.descent: Reverse the North Slopes: downclimb the low-3rd-class/class-2 slabs and talus on the peak's east side back to the col/basin, pick up the braided boot paths back through the Brisingamen Lakelets meadows, and rejoin the Core Zone trail past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes to Aasgard Pass. This is a scramble walk-off in both directions — no rope, rack, or rappelling is used on the standard North Slopes

fktText: Description Little Annapurna is an 8,440 foot tall peak located within the heart of the ever-popular and stunningly beautiful Enchantment Lakes area in Washington state. Summitpost calls Little Annapurna one of the "trademark peaks" of the area because of how frequently it is photographed. The namesake comes from the resemblance of the shape of the south face of the Himalayan peak, Annapurna. From the summit, you have excellent views of Tahoma (Mount Rainier) on a clear day, the entire Enchantment Lakes area, as well as a stunning vantage point to enjoy views of Dragontail and Stuart peaks. The route takes you past the vivid Colchuck Lake and over the notoriously steep Aasgard Pass as well, both of which are popular objectives for day hikers. Note: the Enchantments area is a high-use area. Please stick to established trails as much as possible to reduce impact, and follow all wilderness regulations and rules. The route: This is an out-and-back route, meaning you start at the trailhead, summit, and return to the trailhead. Start from the Stuart and Colchuck Lake Trailhead ( https://maps.app.goo.gl/GD45TEUP3M5TpdY16 ). Follow the obvious trail through dense forest to Colchuck Lake. You'll be able to see Aasgard Pass once you get to the lake – the obvious low point to climber's left of Dragontail Peak. Yes, the pass is as steep as it looks. fktTitle: Mt Adams to Mt Hood (WA, OR)

ours.name: South Climb (South Spur)
ours.approach: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Rd to the Forest Road 23 junction; bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 junction for South Climb, turn left and follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then follow FR 8040 (steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks — no RVs/trailers) for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead (5,600 ft). The trail follows an old roadbed through the burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadows, crosses Round-the-Mountain Trail #9 and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge to the base of the summit snowfields.
ours.descent: Retrace the ascent line: cross back over the shallow summit crater, down over Piker's Peak, and descend the broad snow slopes of Suksdorf/Crescent Ridge to Lunch Counter, then follow the old roadbed back to the trailhead. Glissading is common on the lower snowfields in firm-but-soft conditions; watch for exposed rock and runout hazards in late season as snow recedes.

ours.name: Wilson Glacier Headwall
ours.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. ours.name: Northwest Face/Corner
ours.approach: Same approach as the South Corner (Staircase → Flapjack Lakes → Needle Pass, closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire — see Closures). From Needle Pass, continue along or near the crest of Sawtooth Ridge past the South Corner start line to reach the northwest side of Cruiser's summit pinnacle via exposed 3rd/4th-class ridge scrambling.
ours.descent: After a short exposed class 3 scramble from the summit, rappel the standard South Corner anchors.

fktText: Description https://www.mountaineers.org/activities/routes-places/mount-cruiser-southwest-corner Starting and finishing at Staircase Ranger Station at the Staircase entrance to Olympic National Park. This is a unique climb for the Olympics which includes a 5th class rock climb to the summit. This route is typically done as an overnight trip with a camp at Flapjack Lakes or Gladys Divide. However fast and light it is doable as a day trip. This one has it all, Lush forests, blue rivers, sub alpine lakes, steep snow, and a finish on a 5th class rock climb lands you on the summit of Mount Cruiser, the high point of the Olympics Sawtooths! The approach trail is a bit long from the rock climbers perspective but a pleasant trot to the experienced trail runner. Although very pretty, the route to Flapjack Lakes and onto Gladys Divide doesn’t need much description as it is well established and signed. From Gladys Divide in most seasons the snow fun begins. Needle Pass is obvious from here as “The Needle” looms in its notch. Don crampons here if needed and ascend with axe in hand. If this section actually fully thaws late season I bet its a nasty scree gully and likely its more enjoyable with snow. Once you gain the pass head climbers left and enjoy a good stretch of generally class 2/3 scrambling all the way to where the base of the climb begins. The canon hole is a notable feature on this route and once you get through it, you’ll know, and you are ready to flake the rope and get ready

ours.name: South Corner
ours.approach: From the Staircase Ranger Station (~770-850 ft, at the end of Lake Cushman Rd/North Fork Skokomish Rd), the approach starts on the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, a gently graded old decommissioned roadbed that runs up-valley through old-growth forest for about 3.7-3.8 miles to the former road-end/Spike Camp junction with the Flapjack Lakes Trail. Bear onto the Flapjack Lakes Trail, which climbs steadily and then steeply (with one rough slide/washout bypass to pick through) for about 4 more miles, gaining about 2,000 ft, to reach Flapjack Lakes (~3,850 ft, about 7.5-8 miles from the trailhead) - the standard base camp. ours.descent: Reverse the exposed Class 3 ridge-crest scramble/downclimb back to the top of the technical ground, then begin rappelling. ours.name: Stujack Pass + Summit Scramble
ours.approach: From I-5 exit 208, drive east on SR-530 through Arlington and continue about 28 miles to Darrington. At the four-way stop in town, turn right (south) onto the Mountain Loop Highway and follow it roughly 14 miles — paved, then graveled — to FR-2095 (the Mt. Pugh Spur Road), signed with a large prominent marker on the left. Turn left onto FR-2095 and continue about 1.5 miles to the Mt. Pugh Trailhead (#644) on the right; parking at the trailhead itself is very limited (a handful of cars), so the large pullout at the switchback just below the trailhead is a reliable overflow option. From the trailhead, Trail #644 climbs through deep old-growth forest with several stream crossings, gaining about
ours.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent scramble route back over the Straight Creek Fault notch, chimney, and Knife's Edge ridge to Stujack Pass, then follow Trail #644 back down past Lake Metan to the trailhead. There is no rappelling on the standard route and no fixed rope stations. That said, the descent is not to be taken lightly: several trip reports flag the class 3 chimney/knife-e

fktText: Description Trailhead : Mount Pugh Trailhead (#644), off Forest Road 2095 via the Mountain Loop Highway, ~1,950 ft. Northwest Forest Pass required. Distance/Gain : ~11 miles round trip, ~5,300 ft gain, out-and-back. Route : From the trailhead, forested trail with several stream crossings climbs to Lake Metan at 1.5 miles (3,260 ft), the last water source. Stay left at the lake junction. Long switchbacks continue up through forest and a boulder field to Stujack Pass (~5,700 ft). Beyond the pass, the trail roughens and follows the ridge around a small glacier, leading to an exposed scrambling section known as the Knife's Edge, then hands-on scrambling to the true summit. ours.name: Haystack Scramble
ours.approach: Hike the Mount Si Trail from the SE Mt. Si Road trailhead (Discover Pass) about 4 mi and about 3,150 ft past Snag Flats to Haystack Basin (about 3,900 ft). From the basin meadow, follow the path northeast to the wooden bench at the base of the scramble.
ours.descent: Reverse the route carefully. Downclimb the slabby, exposed moves north to the saddle between the main and north summits, then descend the northeast-facing gully facing in where it steepens. Back at the bench and basin meadow, return about 4 mi down the Mount Si Trail to the trailhead. Many accidents happen on the way down. Take your time and test holds.

fktText: Description Dan Kraft submitted the route: Mount Si is an extremely popular hike near Seattle. Its summit is known as "the Haystack" and is a class 3 scramble. If traveling all the way to the summit, the new trail gains about 3600' in 3.5 miles. The round trip (car-to-car) variation has a Strava segment , but people should report their actual stopwatch time for the FKT. Also, you must do the short scramble to the true summit (some of the Strava times do not include the summit bit). Another route is "Old Si", via the older trail, from the Little Si trailhead to boulder garden cutoff to the old Si trail to the top (first rocky outcrop), with times reported as per this Strava segment (which doesn't include the summit scramble). The Circumnavigation, mostly on CG and FS roads, is about 35 miles with 4900 feet of elevation gain.
